declared.title: Outcome versus process focused future thinking: results from a randomised experiment
declared.foundIn: reports/choose-your-struggle/counter-evidence.md (cards 2 and 6); Crossref search « Hallford outcome-focused process-focused thinking anticipatory pleasure motivation preregistered » (2026-11-26)

population: 134 adults living in Australia (72% women, mean age 35), online, who imagined four pleasant everyday future events, randomly told to focus on outcome or steps

findings.text: Thinking about the outcome of pleasant everyday future events raised anticipatory pleasure, self-reported motivation and personal significance, rated right after the task

support.sentence: Outcome-focused thinking increased anticipatory pleasure, motivation and personal significance.

findings.text: Thinking about the steps lowered perceived control and went with less anticipated and anticipatory pleasure, rated right after the task

support.sentence: In contrast, process-focused thinking reduced perceived control and was associated with reductions in both anticipated and anticipatory pleasure.

limits: self-reported feelings right after the task, one item per event: no effort, behaviour or result measured
four pleasant everyday events (an afternoon in a park, a dinner with a friend, exercise, an achievement), not a hard goal pursued afterwards
the process group did not focus on the steps more than on the outcome (dz = 0.07): the manipulation did not isolate process simulation (the authors say so)
preregistered (AsPredicted); its prediction of more perceived control after thinking about the steps was contradicted (less)
adults living in Australia, recruited online (190 began, 136 finished); 72% women; no sample from the Middle East or North Africa
